title: Speedrun Is Back!! | Sicilian - Alapin | GM Naroditsky's Theory Speedrun

moves.spoken: We play the Sicilian, c5, our real opening.
White develops a knight to f3 and we play d6, heading toward Najdorf waters.
White plays c3 — the delayed Alapin, a relatively harmless anti-Sicilian, but dangerous against an unprepared opponent, like any anti-Sicilian.
The first step is a knight to f6, of course.
White plays h3. One appeal of this line for beginners: a knight grab on e4 loses to a queen check on a4, forking the knight and king — the most commonly missed opening fork. h3 is a sideline.
The main moves are a bishop to b2, or lately the Copc bishop to d3, even a bishop check on b5.
The main move here is a knight to c6.

White plays a bishop to d3 — the Copc system, a weird-looking move until you see the follow-up: he wants to drop the bishop back to c2 and control the center with d4. I'll choose a setup that's less theoretical, even if it's slightly worse.
We play g6 — a Dragon setup. I've played this against Magnus in blitz: allow d4, then attack the center from a distance.
White plays a bishop to c2.
We fianchetto with a bishop to g7.
White castles, allowing us to play e5 — another interesting setup. Which setup you choose as Black is largely a matter of taste.
I like e5, clamping d4 — it strongly discourages d4, and if White plays it anyway, a series of trades reopens our g7 bishop to lord over the long diagonal.

White plays a rook to e1. Don't think of the g7 bishop alone — the bishop and the e5 pawn are a unit exerting control over d4, the key square. The d5 hole is real, but White can't easily occupy it, since our knight guards it.
The drawbacks are real, but the benefits outweigh them here, and we have nice central control.
White commits to d4.
We capture on d4 — that's the whole point.
We take twice — with the pawn, not the knight, which is too committal; then we can decide between grabbing on e4 or a neutral move like a rook to e8.
We recapture on d4 with the pawn — the whole zen of the setup was to take this way if he pushed d4.

White recaptures on d4. d6 is a weakness, but we have real strengths: a development lead, White's undeveloped queenside, our monster g7 bishop, and the e4 pawn as a target for our rook — a structure I know well from the Ruy Lopez.

A rook to e8, keeping the tension. To beat a higher-rated player who knows the fundamentals, force them into hard decisions — which often means quiet improving moves that pass the ball back, not forcing the action, especially in time pressure.
White plays a knight to f3 — a bishop to a4 would be a feeble one-move threat. Now d5 is the direct attempt to erase our biggest weakness.
So d5. The complications peak — either the center opens and our superior bishop and White's undeveloped queenside tell, or White pushes on and we've exploited his lack of development.
My intuition strongly points to d5 — a basic principle, opening the center against the less-developed side, applied in a complex position.
White captures on d5. Very important not to fall asleep and play a knight capture on d5 — that loses a piece.
First we take on e1 — a rook capture threatens the exchange on e8 with the queen overloaded — then, depending on how White recaptures, we take on d5.
A queen capture on d5 would drop the queen to a rook check on c8, since the knight is overloaded.
White recaptures with the queen on e1 — the natural choice, keeping the knight developed — again forcing an unpleasant decision.

We recapture on d5 with the knight — a queen recapture walks into a knight to c3 with tempo. Centralizing, we discourage a knight to c3, and the knight has b4 and d3 in its future. Black has a small edge, and open-center positions are hard for anyone.
White plays a bishop to b3 — a good square. We develop our bishop: a bishop to b6 walks into a knight to g5, so a bishop to f5.
A bishop to f5. The queen isn't overloaded — against a bishop to g5 we move the queen to d7, which also lets a rook come to e8.

White plays a knight to a3, working around the obstacles. The only way to develop the bishop with tempo is a bishop to g5, else b2 hangs — so we want to take the sting out of it with a queen to d7, off the bishop's line.
A queen to d7 — the most natural, getting the queen out of the bishop's fire.
White plays a queen to d1, attacking the knight. A bishop capture on d5 would play into our hands — an unassailable queen on d5, and without that bishop White's position comes unstuck.
A knight to b4 protecting the other knight and preparing a knight to d3 — I'd like to keep the queens on to preserve pressure, though the endgame also looks nasty for White.
I think the queen to d1 was a mistake — only a bishop to g5 held the balance.
White is stuck because of the b2 pawn — nothing moves. He plays a knight to d4, trying to eliminate our g7 bishop, which anchors our whole position.

White sandwiches with a bishop to d3, which actually attacks the knight — the knight is Atlas holding up the world, ripe for an overload, but I don't see one, and a bishop capture on d5 just runs into a queen recapture.
White plays a knight to c2. First question: what's his threat? A bishop capture on d5 is the real problem to defuse.
So a rook to c8, activating our last piece and pressuring the c2 knight — the c-file is where the party is.
White captures on b4.
We recapture on b4 — the knight still protects the bishop, and White still has the problem knight on d4.
a3 was probably White's best move here.
White plays a3 — a panicky reaction. There are crazy complications, and I've found an interesting idea.
A bishop capture on d4 — counterintuitive, but I've calculated a winning line.
Most people would recapture with the queen for the security of a centralized queen, but after the pawn takes our knight, our bishop isn't actually hanging — a bishop capture on f2 with check.
The bishop sacrifice on f2 doesn't work; my idea is a straightforward queen to f5, attacking f2 and piling on the pressure while our time advantage grows.
White plays a queen to e1 — a bishop to e3 was the best try to eliminate our d4 monster. Now a rook to e8 is tempting but a queen capture on c8 is a check, so we need prep.
We play a6, a small improvement, so that when the bishop comes out we grab b2 — a pawn is better than nothing.
White plays a bishop to e3 — the clock is down to thirty seconds and panic is near.
We claim a small prize on b2 — just a pawn, but it always starts with a pawn.
White plays a rook to d1. A bishop to c3 comes close to trapping the queen, but he has a bishop to d2.
A bishop to c3 — the bishop was offside on b2.
A bishop to d4, testing our opponent — we can always repeat, which isn't a draw since we can vary.
Let's keep it simple with a bishop to c3.
We trade the dark-squared bishops on d2 to keep our winning chances alive.
White recaptures with the queen. Now a bishop to c2 is smart — after the trade it's a rook endgame a pawn up, very hard for White to hold in time pressure.
A bishop to c2, forcing the bishop trade.
White captures on c2 — and I've blundered g4 here, I realize.
We recapture on c2 — that recapture might have been a blunder.
g4 might have just forced a draw for White.
g4 was blundered by me — bad — but our opponent missed it, so we keep torturing White.
First, the rook has overstayed on c8 — reposition it to e8.
A huge blunder: I should have gone back to c4 with the bishop instead of c2, forgetting g4 — a sloppy moment.
White plays a queen to d5. I like the queen trade — it makes defense even harder for White, and trading on the right square while hitting a pawn is even better.
A queen to e4 catches my eye — create problems every move, force decisions in the last seconds.
White plays a queen to c5. We play a waiting game, hoping for a blunder.
We play h5, improving slowly and forcing another decision as White's clock dwindles.
A rook to e6 — I see a trap; I'm hoping for a check and then a rook to d8.

White checks on d8, the king steps to g7, and White finally trades queens. We're winning: a pawn up, and White's king is cut off along the e-file. The plan: a king to e5, and a rook to c6 forcing a rook trade with our king covering every escape square, then we go after the b-pawn and promote — our pawns are perfectly configured with no kingside passer for White. He resigns.
I'm really upset about missing g4 — the bishop to c2 should have lost the game.
It was a genuine blunder.
The engine's move was a bishop to c4, as I originally intended.
But I played a bishop to c2 — the point being that the queen and rook are the worst defenders, the easiest pieces to attack.
I completely missed g4 — the only way to keep the bishop defended is a queen to e4...
...but then the c8 rook loses its defender.
After g4, a queen to e4, and a rook to c1, Black suddenly loses — the rook is unprotected, the bishop is under fire.
The best practical option would have been a queen to f3.
I'd have played a queen to f3 with two pieces and two pawns for the piece and a weak white king — only plus one, not completely winning.
After a queen to e2, a queen to c3 forks the bishop and the pawn — still a game, but White is in the driver's seat.
It looks easy when I hand-feed it, but it's an elementary tactic I missed.

Blunders happen — everyone commits them. As for the opening: this is the delayed Alapin, because the regular Alapin is the immediate c3 — and a move played one tempo later leads to a completely different position, so don't compare the two.
